newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar says missing EMU spells less jobs.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar says missing EMU spells less jobs.

text.p: Spain's Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said on Wednesday failure to enter Europe's monetary union would deepen Spain's unemployment -- currently the highest in Europe.

"The cost of not entering a monetary union would be much worse because we would enter a path of high inflation, interest rates and debt, and therefore higher unemployment," Aznar told local news agency Europa press in an interview.

But a number of analysts disagreed that joining Europe's monetary union (EMU) would benefit employment and said the notoriously rigid labour market would hamper any gains that EMU may hold for jobs in the medium term.

"If you can't devalue and you have unemployment problems then you either need to subsidise those areas of the economy that are not doing well or have a very flexible labour market and Spain has a very rigid labour market," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
According to the National Statistics Institute, Spain's unemployment stood at 21.91 percent in the third quarter, double the European Union average.
The government has recognised that labour market reforms are vital to ease joblessness, but economists said it was unlikely that such reforms would go far enough before EMU's planned start in 1999.
"The government will approach reforms fairly cautiously and it is not in a position where it can ram through too many unpopular measures," said one analyst in London.
"What the government needs to do is to tackle the actual bedrock of legislation and make it simpler and more flexible," he added.
The start of Spain's labour reform effort is expected to get under way at the start of 1997 with unions and businessmen meeting to agree an accord.
As far as higher interest rates and debt are concerned, analysts agreed that financial markets would certainly scold Spain if it was not part of EMU.
"From the financial markets point of view he is right up to a point that Spain would be punished if it did not make EMU, with higher interest rates and a greater deficit," said Lumholdt.
